facts.text: Before settlers, the land of New Union belonged to the Cherokee Nation, but the 1830 Indian Removal Act opened it for farming after the Trail of Tears.
Around 1840, farmers from neighboring states flooded New Union’s plateau, attracted by fertile soils ideal for cotton and subsistence farming.
New Union sits on Sand Mountain’s plateau, with elevations ranging from 466 to 1,634 feet and an average of 768 feet.
The town experiences a humid subtropical climate, moderate radon, and air quality near national averages, yet it is prone to tornadoes and floods.
Today New Union’s economy centers on services, retail trade, and health care, with common jobs in office support, maintenance, and sales.
New Union lies about 45 miles northeast of Huntsville and 54 miles east of Birmingham, nestled near the Appalachian foothills.
